newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's Kolodko unveils his EMU membership plan.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Kolodko unveils his EMU membership plan.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko on Tuesday invited journalists to an Irish pub to treat them to a pint of stout priced in Ecu as he unveiled his plan for Poland's European Monetary Union membership.

Kolodko said Poland stood a chance of meeting all EMU criteria and benefitting from full European integration early next century. He said his plan "Euro 2006" was spelling out what Poland could gain and what it had to do to gain entry.

Kolodko said he decided to hold a news conference in an Irish pub after a EU summit in Dublin, to get across a message that if Poles were persistent enough they could be paying for their beer in new European currency in less than 10 years.

"We are meeting in the Irish Pub because the last EU summit was held in Dublin and...Irish people were then assured that the euro would buy as much stout as the punt and I hope that this will be also the case with Poland," Kolodko said.

He said his Euro 2006, which has been approved by the government's committee for European Integration and was likely to be debated by the cabinet late this month, should start a nationwide debate on Poland's European ambitions.

"If we held a parliamentary vote now on whether we want full EMU membership by the year say 2004 it could be a unanimous yes. But one has to realise that there are several hard decisions to be made," Kolodko said.
He said EMU membership would allow Polish companies to significantly reduce transaction costs and become more competitive, winning the Polish economy a bigger share in international trade.
But it would also mean that Poland would give up its exchange rate policy as a macreoeconomic tool and yield monetary policy making powers to a European central bank.

He said Poland was already roughly on target with EMU's criteria on the budget gap at slightly above the three percent ceiling calculated according to EU standards and a public debt to GDP ratio comfortably below the 60 percent target.

But meeting inflation, interest rate and currency stability targets would require deep structural reforms, notably the overhaul of Poland's inefficient social security system, and persistence in reducing inflation.

Kolodko's plan assumes a fall in budget deficits to two percent of GDP in 2006 from estimated 2.4 percent in 1997. The plan envisages however higher deficits in 1997-1999 of up to three percent as the treasury expects to assume some extra costs of launching the social security reform.

Public debt is seen falling to 40 percent of GDP in 2006 from last year's 54 percent and 49.8 percent expected this year. Inflation is seen reaching a single digit figure in 1998 after falling to 13 percent this year from estimated 18.4 percent in 1996 and hitting five percent in 2000.
But Kolodko said Poland would be able to meet the Maastricht treaty target, now at 2.6 percent only in 2005.
He said a faster disinflation would require radical tightening which could hamper Poland's growth.
"We could meet inflation goals faster but we want to achieve them while maintaining a healthy rate of growth," he said.
